days.title: Address Spaces, VMAs, Page Tables, and the TLB

questions.prompt: What does a VMA add beyond Linux 0.12's start_code, end_data, brk, and start_stack fields?
options: A physical frame address for every byte
A range with its own protection and backing, so mmap can name more than code, heap, and stack
The TLB entry for that range
A copy of the file's inode data
questions.explanation: Linux 0.12 described the user map with a handful of task fields inside one segment slot. A VMA is one range of virtual addresses with protection and a backing, which is what an arbitrary mmap needs.

questions.prompt: What does the TLB cache?
options: Recent virtual-to-physical translations
The bytes of the mapped file
The VMA red-black tree
The process's file-descriptor table
questions.explanation: The TLB holds translations the CPU has already walked. The file bytes live in page-cache or anonymous pages. A stale TLB entry can still grant an old translation after a PTE change, which is why the kernel invalidates it.

questions.prompt: What does /proc/self/maps report for the lab's untouched anonymous mapping?
options: The physical frame number
A VMA the kernel exported for this process, with Size matching the page and Rss still 0
Proof that the page tables were never allocated
The glibc heap threshold
questions.explanation: maps and smaps are a process-level export of VMAs and accounting. The lab checks that its one-page mapping is present and not resident yet. That export is not a dump of PTEs or physical addresses.

questions.prompt: Why does ToyOS call invlpg after installing a page-table entry?
options: To allocate the physical frame
To drop a translation the CPU might already have cached for that address
To switch to another process
To write the page back to disk
questions.explanation: map_page in projects/toyos/src/memory.c stores the PTE and then executes invlpg. The store changes the table. The invalidation changes what the CPU is allowed to keep using.

days.title: Page Faults, Demand Paging, and Zero-Fill

questions.prompt: The lab's first load of a fresh anonymous page returns which byte, and why?
options: Whatever the previous owner left in the frame
0, because a not-present anonymous page is filled with zeroes rather than leftover frame contents
The page-size value
EOF
questions.explanation: Demand zero-fill is the contract. Linux 0.12's do_no_page took the empty-page path past the executable image. Linux 6.12's do_anonymous_page still has a zero-fill path, including the shared zero page for a read.

questions.prompt: Why does the suite accept any minor-fault delta of at least 1, instead of an exact count?
options: getrusage is not implemented on Linux
ru_minflt counts minor faults for the process between the two calls, and other activity can add faults
A minor fault is always a disk read
The delta includes other processes on the machine
questions.explanation: The marker fault_count_caveat is part of the test. RUSAGE_SELF is this process, not the whole machine, and it is not a count of one C statement.

questions.prompt: Which Linux 0.12 path handles a not-present fault?
options: page_fault in mm/page.s calls do_no_page
un_wp_page always runs
sys_brk allocates the frame before returning
The fault is ignored
questions.explanation: The assembly entry tests the error code. A not-present fault goes to do_no_page. A protection fault goes to do_wp_page. brk in that kernel only moves the break.

questions.prompt: Why can a user file fault sleep when a hard interrupt handler must not?
options: The fault always runs with interrupts disabled
Bringing in a file page may wait for I/O, and reclaim under an allocation may wait for writeback
Sleep is required for every TLB miss
The handler is not allowed to read registers
questions.explanation: Week 12's blocking read slept until bytes could move. filemap_fault can sleep for the same reason. That sleep is legal in a user fault and illegal in hard-interrupt context. This is why the fault path is the foundation for later scheduler and interrupt work.

days.title: mmap, mprotect, COW, and Shared Mappings

questions.prompt: What did the lab observe after the child stored through MAP_SHARED?
options: The parent still saw the original byte
The parent saw the child's byte, because both mappings name the same page
The child received SIGSEGV
The file was truncated
questions.explanation: MAP_SHARED means the store updates the shared page. The parent observes it after wait. That is the same page-cache relationship Week 12 showed with pread, now seen across fork.

questions.prompt: What did the parent observe after the child stored through MAP_PRIVATE?
options: The parent's byte stayed the original value
The parent's byte became the child's value
Both processes were killed
The mapping was unmapped
questions.explanation: A private write copies. The child's pipe note shows the child did store. The parent's mapping kept the original byte. Linux 0.12 already had this shape in copy_page_tables and un_wp_page, without mmap.

questions.prompt: Why is the mprotect write a SIGSEGV in the child rather than a copy-on-write?
options: MAP_PRIVATE always signals
PROT_READ removed write permission from the VMA, so the fault is forbidden rather than a request to copy
The page was swapped out
fork does not copy page tables
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write applies when the VMA allows the write and the PTE is not yet writable. mprotect changed the VMA. The parent only reads, survives, and decodes a signaled wait status.

questions.prompt: In Linux 6.12, which do_fault branch is a private writable file fault?
options: do_cow_fault
do_shared_fault
do_anonymous_page only
oom_kill_process
questions.explanation: do_fault sends a read to do_read_fault, a private write to do_cow_fault, and a shared write to do_shared_fault. File data still comes through vm_ops->fault, and filemap_fault is the page-cache implementation. Those names are from commit adc218676eef.

days.title: User Allocators, brk, mmap, and Lifetime

questions.prompt: What does Linux 0.12 sys_brk do with the new break?
options: It allocates and zeroes every new page before returning
It records the break when the address is in range. The page is created later by the fault
It maps a file
It runs the buddy allocator
questions.explanation: The syscall updates current->brk inside the gap below the stack. do_no_page's empty-page path is what zero-fills a later access. Linux 6.12 still separates brk, which calls do_brk_flags, from the fault that fills a page.

questions.prompt: Why does the lab refuse to assert a glibc mmap threshold?
options: malloc never calls mmap
The threshold is libc policy and can change. This run's brk and maps lines are observations
The kernel has no brk syscall
sbrk is undefined
questions.explanation: The marker glibc_mmap_threshold_asserted=no is part of the test. A small object landing in [heap] and a large one in an anonymous mapping, or the reverse, would both be legal observations.

questions.prompt: What does munmap change for the lab's explicit mapping?
options: It keeps the VMA and only clears the bytes
The address is no longer in /proc/self/maps
It converts the mapping to MAP_SHARED
It moves the break
questions.explanation: munmap drops that VMA. The lab checks the address is absent afterward. A later access would be a new fault against whatever mapping, if any, occupies the address then.

questions.prompt: What is the ToyOS heap relative to brk and mmap?
options: A bump pointer over a fixed number of mapped pages, without a user brk syscall or a free of individual objects
A full buddy allocator with NUMA nodes
glibc malloc running in ring 3
A swap-backed stack
questions.explanation: Week 7 maps HEAP_PAGES at HEAP_BASE and bumps heap_next. That teaches ownership of mapped pages. It does not teach the libc choice between brk and mmap.

days.title: Physical Pages, Zones, the Buddy Allocator, and NUMA

questions.prompt: What does a buddy split produce?
options: Two power-of-two blocks, one of which can satisfy a smaller order
A single page from a linear scan of mem_map
A VMA
A swap slot
questions.explanation: The simulator starts from one high-order block and splits until the request fits, then coalesces a free block with its buddy. Linux 0.12's get_free_page scanned mem_map for one page and could not hand out this family of sizes.

questions.prompt: Why does the teaching allocator keep ZONE_DMA off the GFP_KERNEL path?
options: DMA memory is faster for every allocation
A device that cannot address all of physical memory needs a reserved low range, so ordinary allocations leave it alone
ZONE_DMA is the NUMA fallback
The buddy cannot allocate from ZONE_NORMAL
questions.explanation: Linux 6.12's comment on zone_type says ZONE_DMA exists for devices with a limited address range, and ZONE_NORMAL is ordinary memory. The lab's rule is a teaching policy, not the kernel's full fallback list.

questions.prompt: What does numa_fallback mean in this lab?
options: The host migrated a page to another CPU socket
The simulator's local zone could not satisfy the order, so it took a block from the other node's same zone
The process was moved by the scheduler
An OOM kill of task_b
questions.explanation: The program never calls mbind, migrate_pages, or any host allocator. host_pages_untouched=yes is a required marker. Distance in the simulator is an integer node id.

questions.prompt: Why did the order-3 DMA allocation fail even though free DMA pages remained on node 0?
options: The free pages were not one aligned block of that order
GFP_DMA is defined to fail
The buddy never splits
NUMA fallback is disabled for every request
questions.explanation: An earlier order-1 allocation split the node-0 DMA zone, and the other node's DMA zone was already taken. Free pages that are not a single high-order buddy cannot satisfy a larger order. The marker is exhausted_alloc=fail.

questions.prompt: Before the simulator reuses a frame that holds a dirty file page, what must it do?
options: Drop the page and lose the store
Write the page back, then drop it
Swap it to the anonymous swap device
Kill task_b immediately
questions.explanation: The dirty store is the only copy of a change that belongs in the file. writeback_count=1 and evict_dirty_file=writeback_then_drop record that step. A clean file page can be dropped because the file can supply it again.

questions.prompt: Why does an anonymous victim need a swap slot in this model?
options: Anonymous memory has no file that can supply the bytes again
Anonymous pages are always clean
The TLB requires a slot number
File pages cannot be evicted
questions.explanation: A file page has a backing. An anonymous page's bytes live only in the frame unless they are written to swap. The simulator has two slots and records swapout_count=2.

questions.prompt: What did the simulator do when the next anonymous eviction found swap full?
options: It killed a host process
It forced the machine to swap
It selected task_b as a simulated OOM choice and left the resident anonymous page in place
It wrote the anonymous page back to a file
questions.explanation: oom_kills_host_process=no and reclaim_host=no are required. Linux 0.12's oom() exited the current task. Linux 6.12's out_of_memory selects a victim. This lab does neither to the host.

questions.prompt: Which Linux 6.12 functions are the real reclaim path the simulator is not running?
options: try_to_free_pages, shrink_folio_list, pageout, and add_to_swap
dup and do_dup2
only sys_brk
invlpg in ToyOS
questions.explanation: Those names are in mm/vmscan.c at commit adc218676eef. try_to_unmap finds the PTEs, and swap_writepage moves an anonymous page. The lab's four-frame LRU is a policy sketch of that idea.

days.title: VM Observation and a Debugging Report

questions.prompt: Which observation belongs only to this process?
options: /proc/vmstat pgfault
/proc/self/maps, smaps, and status
The buddy simulator's node 1
A system-wide swap total
questions.explanation: The core lab reads /proc/self. vmstat_scope=system_wide is printed only by the optional tool, and the report says those counters are the whole machine.

questions.prompt: What is a SKIP from perf or vmstat?
options: A failed core test
Proof the kernel has no page faults
An optional observation that was missing or denied. The deterministic suite does not require it
A request to raise memory pressure until the counter moves
questions.explanation: make tools and the day-7 wrapper treat a missing or denied tool as SKIP. They do not allocate until the machine reclaims.

questions.prompt: What does a passing Week 13 wrapper establish?
options: Mastery of the Linux reclaim subsystem
That the prepared checks ran and the stated limits still apply
That the host kernel is exactly commit adc218676eef
That glibc's allocator threshold is universal
questions.explanation: The overview's checkpoint says finishing the wrappers does not complete mastery. uname on the host can differ from the pinned source tree. Quote symbols only from the tree you opened.

questions.prompt: What does ToyOS record for an injected unmapped write?
options: A demand-zero page and a retry
A diagnosed page fault, including the serial EXPECTED-FAULT line, not a reclaim scan
An OOM kill of another task
A buddy split
questions.explanation: arch.c recognizes vector 14 as a page fault and can print EXPECTED-FAULT. Week 7 does not fill the page and continue. That difference is the point of comparing ToyOS with Linux demand paging.
